title: Helix Analytics POC — Week 3 caching sync
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on cache hit-rate diagnostics and immediate tuning: current KV/prefix cache hit rates are below expectations (approx 22-27%), root causes appear to be prompt variability and user-specific tokens. Team agreed on normalization + key-simplification approach, a dedupe/preprocessing job, and a benchmark run next week. Redwood to provide config patch and deck; Helix to run a small dedupe job and share sample prompts.
next_steps: Redwood: push config patch for prefix-keying + TTL adjustments by 2025-09-13
Helix: run prompt-normalization/dedupe job on 50k historical prompts and share summary by 2025-09-16
Schedule follow-up sync 2025-09-19 to review benchmark and adjust rollouts
action_items: Maya Singh - prepare and share small README + patched redis/key-schema config by 2025-09-13
Tara Chen - run prompt dedupe/normalization on sample of 50k prompts and upload results to shared sheet by 2025-09-16
Eli Romero - run local simulation to estimate hit-rate impact of template_id based keying and report by 2025-09-15
Jon Park - coordinate resource window for controlled benchmark on 2025-09-18 and ensure logs/ingestion enabled
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-09-11 16:00 PDT | Duration: 45 minutes | Attendees: Jordan Price, Maya Singh, Eli Romero, Sam Kaur; Tara Chen, Marcus Alvarez, Priya Nair, Jon Park

[00:00] Jordan Price: alright everybody uh let's get started, thanks for joining the week three sync on the cache work for the Helix pilot. quick check in — anyone got any blockers?
[00:12] Tara Chen: no blockers, just curious to see the numbers you pulled, we've been nervously watching those hit rates.
[00:18] Maya Singh: yeah sure, we'll jump into that. quick note — transcription might mangle some names.
[00:22] Marcus Alvarez: that's fine.

[00:30] Maya Singh: ok so slide one — raw numbers from the last 72 hours: KV cache hit-rate is hovering 23% overall, prefix cache is a bit higher in certain templates around 31%, but when we exclude debug/test traffic it drops to ~27%.
[00:45] Tara Chen: wow that's lower than expected. we were hoping for 50%+ after the first tuning pass.
[00:50] Eli Romero: right, and we dug into the keys — a lot of variance comes from user-specific tokens and session ids being embedded in the prompt body. so the key space exploded.
[01:05] Priya Nair: can you give an example?
[01:08] Eli Romero: sure — we saw many prompts like "summarize user123's week" or logs that include timestamps and ephemeral IDs, so every request becomes unique. the cache key is currently the full prompt hash in the default POC config.
[01:22] Tara Chen: ah — that explains it. our app often appends a small audit header to every prompt.

[01:30] Jordan Price: two high-level approaches: normalization (strip/noise tokens, canonicalize placeholders) or change key-space (use template_id + normalized context hash instead of full prompt). both have tradeoffs.
[01:43] Marcus Alvarez: tradeoffs meaning accuracy vs cache-ability?
[01:46] Maya Singh: yes — if you normalize too aggressively you might lose intent nuance — e.g., user locale or time references — which can change outputs. but for many of your query templates, the variable bits are not material to the model's response.

[02:02] Jon Park: on the infra side we also noticed frequent small objects causing memory churn. eviction is LRU and TTL is 1 hour right now. with the current cardinality, objects churn every few minutes.
[02:14] Eli Romero: so suggested immediate wins: 1) implement prompt normalization rules to strip session IDs and noise headers, 2) switch keying to template_id + truncated normalized hash for ephemeral fields, 3) increase per-shard capacity / bump TTL temporarily during benchmark.

[02:30] Tara Chen: ok what's the fastest to test?
[02:33] Maya Singh: normalization + simple key rewrite is quickest — few lines in preprocessor. we can ship a patch to your staging by Friday.
[02:38] Jordan Price: we'll also include a config flag to opt into prefix-keying so you can roll back if needed.

[02:44] Marcus Alvarez: is there any risk with compliance? we need to preserve PII handling.
[02:48] Maya Singh: yes, don't normalize PII in a way that removes redaction markers, and we'll follow your redaction pipeline. the normalization job should run after redaction so no raw PII is used.

[03:00] Priya Nair: what's the expected delta? if we hit 60% that's huge. what is realistic?
[03:05] Eli Romero: based on our sims on your sample datasets, switching to template-based keys + normalization gave us a modeled lift from 25% to about 58-63% on templated traffic. open queries with lots of free text will stay low.
[03:20] Tara Chen: and what's the impact on latency?
[03:22] Maya Singh: negligible — cache hit avoids token generation cost entirely, so client latency improves for hits; slightly more CPU at preprocessing but that's small.

[03:35] Jordan Price: other levers — prefetching top-N responses for common templates, intelligent eviction (priority backlog for business-critical templates), and batching small requests. but those are medium-term. quick wins are normalization + key change.

[03:50] Jon Park: question: can Redwood provide an instrumented run for us to compare with our logs? we want token-level breakdowns.
[03:56] Jordan Price: yes, we'll enable detailed token/route trace for the benchmark window and share dashboards. console will show token cost, hit/miss, and latency percentiles.

[04:10] Tara Chen: what's in the config patch you mentioned?
[04:12] Maya Singh: patch will include: (a) a toggle to use template_id keying, (b) normalization rules sample (regexes to strip session ids and timestamps), (c) suggested TTL bump from 1h to 3h for the benchmark, (d) logging hooks to capture normalized vs raw prompt hashes for verification.

[04:30] Marcus Alvarez: timeline?
[04:32] Maya Singh: we'll push the patch by 2025-09-13; you test on staging; Tara runs the normalization/dedupe on the 50k sample by 2025-09-16; then we run the 100k controlled benchmark on 2025-09-18. follow up on 2025-09-19.

[04:45] Priya Nair: can the dedupe job be destructive? we can't mutate production prompts.
[04:50] Eli Romero: we'll run dedupe as read-only analysis first — generate canonical forms and counts, no writes. you can opt to run a rewrite in a separate migration.

[05:00] Jordan Price: ok let's look at one concrete anomalous example from the sheet — prompt id 13,492: includes a 10-char session token mid-string which prevented a hit for 284 duplicated templates.
[05:12] Tara Chen: yeah that one is from an internal connector we forgot about.
[05:15] Marcus Alvarez: is there a recommended canonical key format?
[05:18] Maya Singh: we usually recommend [template_id]|[normalized_context_hash:8]|[slot_signature], where normalized_context_hash is computed after removing noise tokens and lowercasing. that keeps keys small and stable.

[05:35] Jon Park: will that affect eviction sizing? if the key is smaller maybe we store more entries in the same memory footprint?
[05:40] Eli Romero: yes smaller keys = smaller metadata footprint; but payload size (response tokens) dominates memory. still helpful. Also consider compressing stored payloads or limiting stored tokens to the first N tokens if acceptable.

[06:00] Tara Chen: examples of unacceptable normalization?
[06:03] Maya Singh: removing locale or instruction tokens that actually change semantics — e.g., "summarize in Spanish" — don't remove language tags. remove only audit/session/timestamp noise.

[06:20] Marcus Alvarez: on metrics, what should we watch besides hit-rate?
[06:23] Jordan Price: hit-rate, per-route cost, tail latency (p95/p99), and quality regression (we'll run a small eval set to ensure normalization doesn't drop quality). also cache fill rate and eviction churn.

[06:38] Tara Chen: are there known gotchas with tokenization that affects hashing?
[06:42] Eli Romero: yes — differences in whitespace, unicode normalization, and punctuation can change tokenizer outputs and so the normalized hash must run the same tokenizer code as the runtime. we'll include a canonicalizer in the patch.

[06:55] Maya Singh: also note that small changes in templates (like adding a helper word) will split keys; we recommend template versioning so keys incorporate template_id:v2 for a structured rollout.

[07:10] Jordan Price: ok, practical plan: Maya will ship patch with normalization + key toggle; Eli will run local sim; Tara will run dedupe analysis; Jon will provision infra for the benchmark. after the benchmark we'll look at token-level cost and decide on rollout to production.

[07:28] Priya Nair: can we have Redwood run a short A/B for the template-keying versus full-prompt-keying? say 10% traffic?
[07:33] Maya Singh: yes we have native rollout controls — canary the keying for a percentage of traffic and automatically rollback on error. we'll include a canary config in the patch.

[07:45] Marcus Alvarez: one small ask — please also send us a short doc on how this affects our compliance logs and auditability.
[07:50] Jordan Price: absolutely — Sam will attach a short compliance note explaining redaction order and retained metadata.

[07:58] Tara Chen: any implications for Dedicated / Private deployment? we may move to dedicated later.
[08:02] Eli Romero: same approach works for Dedicated; keying logic is client-side so behavior is consistent across hosted/dedicated/private. we may recommend different TTLs depending on memory.

[08:15] Jordan Price: ok let's capture next steps —
[08:17] Sam Kaur: I'll add them to the CRM and follow up with calendar invites.

[08:22] Jordan Price: quick Q about quality monitoring — we will hook your eval set to Redwood Optimize so any regressions after normalization trigger alerts.
[08:29] Tara Chen: perfect.

[08:35] Jordan Price: anything else before we wrap?
[08:38] Priya Nair: just please include the sample regexes; our infra team will review for false positives.
[08:44] Maya Singh: will do.

[08:48] Jordan Price: great. thanks everyone — we'll share the patch and deck after the call. see you at the benchmark sync.

[44:50] Jordan Price: meeting adjourned.

Notes: transcript contains minor transcription errors (names may be spelled differently in live transcript). Refer to shared links for raw logs and the analysis spreadsheet.
